title: The Trader Who Never Spoke...Until Now - Open Interest - Ep.19

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Trader Who Never Spoke...Until Now - Open Interest - Ep.19.docx

summary:
Open Interest ep.19: Drew describes Tactical's systematic futures method designed to sit opposite commercial hedgers (risk premium capture, price-based algorithms from COT patterns), not trend following, though it correlates with trend followers.
Stresses timing, money management and portfolio selection, with portfolio construction by orthogonal sectors/markets most important.
Also small-fund capacity advantage in small markets and investor alignment; Seykota is discretionary pattern trader.

coverage.note: scared money advice, starting a fund, ER career
Tactical edge: hedger risk premia; not a trend trader
zero-sum, who wins and loses (COT groups), hedger transfer
COT patterns used to design timing algorithm
algorithm used for 40 years; hedging in currencies, rates, equities
equity futures excluded; timing vs money management; sizing and stops
correlated market sizing, robustness tests, goals of portfolio
investors first; small markets and capacity
fund size cap, capacity, new markets

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - first reader caught the central hedger-premium method, three-part system framework, portfolio orthogonality and business-model points; missed several supporting reasoning steps and two speaker attributions were wrong.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: Futures trading is a zero sum game. That is got to be understood by anyone who is trying to to, you know, be successful in the markets.
claims.claim: Futures profits come from someone else's losses, so a trader should know who is losing money for them to make it.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: if you take this job, you're going to trade with your own money. I know it. And it's going to be scared money.
claims.claim: Trade with money you can afford to lose from an independent income source; scared money forces poor decisions.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: to do this right, you really need a lot of money to diversify properly. So, why not start a fund?
claims.claim: Proper diversification across many futures markets requires more capital than an individual typically has, which motivated starting a fund.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: Ed has uh of course certain very um welldefined rules in his mind for trading.
claims.claim: Ed Seykota's style is computer-assisted technical discretionary pattern-based trading, not algorithmic trend following; he knows system strengths and weaknesses from backtests but uses computers for data display and cleaning.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: We always felt that our edge was capturing risk premia from hedggers and we designed our system specifically to do that.
claims.claim: Tactical's edge was capturing risk premia from commercial hedgers; because that profit appears mainly when markets trend, returns correlate highly with trend followers.
claims.conditions: works in futures with true hedging flows; not in equity futures
claims.testable: partly - COT-based hedger position strategies are testable

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: only the big speculators over time take money out of the markets. The commercial hedgers lose money in the futures markets and the small speculators lose money in the futures markets.
claims.claim: Academic studies show that only large speculators earn profits over time while commercial hedgers and small speculators lose, so a professional must take money from hedgers.
claims.indicator: COT trader groups: large speculators, small speculators, commercial hedgers
claims.conditions: size makes small speculators irrelevant as a source

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: those hedggers have traded opposite you at some point. The price got high enough for them to
claims.claim: A trend follower implicitly takes money from hedgers: a farmer hedges when price is high enough, then loses on futures as the trend continues while locking in profit on physical crops.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: and you could see where the big the big specs and the hedggers shifted from net long to net short and vice versa.
claims.claim: In the 1980s, COT data (two-week lag) was used to find chart patterns that precede shifts in hedger net positions, and price-based algorithms were built from these patterns rather than using COT data in the live system.
claims.indicator: CFTC Commitments of Traders, price patterns
claims.conditions: only worked when futures were the main hedging venue
claims.testable: partly - derived rules reproducible only with price patterns

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: the futures markets were really the only vehicles that big commercial hedgers had that were liquid enough for them to hedge their positions.
claims.claim: The hedger-opposite method stopped being reproducible because hedgers now have OTC and options routes to lay off risk, so futures positions no longer capture their flows.
claims.testable: no - structural claim, hard to test

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: systematic trading is also discretionary, but the discretion it goes in at the front.
claims.claim: Systematic trading involves discretion at design (choice of rules) and none afterwards; the same timing algorithms from 1984 were used until the fund closed in 2023, without overriding.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: it's absolutely a valid model in those
claims.claim: The hedger model applies to currencies (institutions laying off risk) and to interest rate futures but breaks down at the short end of the curve where central bank arbitrage dominates; equity futures excluded because tied to index arbitrage so no genuine price discovery by hedgers.
claims.indicator: hedging flows in currencies, rates, equities

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: in a system of trading there are three main aspects. There's timing, there's money management and there's portfolio selection
claims.claim: A trading system has three separable parts (timing, money management, portfolio selection); entries came from opposite-hedger timing, exits from money-management rules, and the system was not always in the market.
claims.testable: partly - components can be tested separately

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: we sized our positions based on the uh uh likelihood that that position would get stopped out with just a random movement of price
claims.claim: Positions were sized by volatility so that a trailing stop is not triggered by random price noise (ATR-like), giving the market enough room but not too much.
claims.testable: yes - ATR sizing and trailing stop backtest

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: I felt that this style of trading was inherently going to have a swingy uh type of equity stream because I'm taking what the hedgers don't want.
claims.claim: Taking risk hedgers want to shed gives a volatile equity stream with frequent small losses and occasional large wins, the opposite of an insurer's income profile; drawdowns must be expected.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: I tested absolutely every single thing under the sun. I had computers going 247 for years testing every possible system
claims.claim: The original timing algorithm proved robust for 40 years after extensive testing of alternatives, which Drew programmed himself so he could ask complex portfolio-level questions.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: we did not have such a um a a rule in the uh system.
claims.claim: There was no maximum portfolio heat rule; large open equity did not trigger cutting positions, and the computer helps follow trades during long drawdowns though psychological pain remains.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: the portfolio is an order of magnitude at least 10 times more important than either of the other two.
claims.claim: Portfolio selection matters more than timing or money management; the same system on cocoa versus crude oil gives very different outcomes, so portfolio construction deserves the most attention.
claims.testable: partly - compare portfolio choices on the same system

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: markets are fractal over a wide range. If you get too short or you get too long, the fractal nature of markets breaks down.
claims.claim: The same hedger-shift pattern was applied across multiple time frames because markets are self-similar over a range, and backtests confirmed it.
claims.conditions: breaks down at extreme short or long time frames

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: You have to have some rule to tell you when to stop trading a certain market.
claims.claim: Portfolios need rules for adding new markets (e.g. heating oil before crude futures) and removing dying ones (potato futures), including how long to wait before trusting a new market.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: you have to construct it with this goal in mind. And you have to say, I want orthogonal markets
claims.claim: If the portfolio goal is smooth equity growth, choose orthogonal markets; 25 interest-rate futures give almost no smoothing, so weights by sector and sub-sector should reflect correlations.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: ever so slowly make adjustments over time if markets no longer were behaving in the way that we had initially assessed them
claims.claim: Weights are set top-down by sectors and sub-sectors using orthogonality and slowly updated if correlations change.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: look back as far as I could over time or write a program, analyze the results, and then break it up in little segments of of yearly intervals, rolling intervals
claims.claim: Design questions (e.g. half weights for correlated petroleum markets versus full weight on first signal) should be tested over rolling 5- and 10-year blocks to see if the answer is robust.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: I want a portfolio that has the markets in it that have the best potential to make money in the near term. And so then you have to have some type of an algorithm that gives a relative strength weight
claims.claim: Alternative portfolio goal: hold only the best markets by relative strength (e.g. top five), requiring an algorithm that changes weights as strength changes; Tactical instead sought smoothness.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: the people who got really big, they spent a significant amount of money on marketing and the investors paid for it uh one way or another
claims.claim: Marketing costs of large funds are paid by investors via commissions or fees, creating misalignment; smaller funds with investors-first philosophy avoided this.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: If you are smaller, you can operate in some of these smaller markets. And some of these smaller markets are the really diversifying ones.
claims.claim: Smaller funds can trade small orthogonal markets (lumber, orange juice, cotton, cocoa, sugar) that a $10bn fund cannot, giving more diversification and less noise than large funds concentrated in rates and equities.
claims.direction: diversification benefit up for smaller funds

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: We've even put language in our legal offering documents that will limit the size of the fund
claims.claim: Capping fund size keeps access to small markets; individual trades lose 70% of the time, but adding canola to the 10-year note helps the portfolio much more than adding the five-year note.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the legal offering-document cap, the 70% losing trades statement and the canola versus 5-year note comparison are Moritz Seibert describing his own fund (Drew's Tactical had already closed).
correction.fix: Seibert caps his fund's size in the offering documents so it can keep trading small markets such as lumber, oats and canola; individual trades in these markets lose about 70% of the time, but adding canola to the 10-year note helps the portfolio much more than adding the 5-year note.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: If you have a billion, 2 billion, three billion of assets under management, the investors demand you to have that.
claims.claim: Large AUM brings institutional staffing and due-diligence burdens that pull focus from trading; investors in drawdown tend to redeem at lows, so screening for the right investors improves outcomes.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: need 3 years to get out of an interest rate, you know, credit derivative swap contract
claims.claim: Liquid futures strategies can return capital within about 30 days, so key-person risk is less costly than for illiquid strategies; Tactical closed in 2023 when two key employees retired.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker and claim: the liquidity and key-person argument (monthly liquidity, no 3-year swap exit) is Moritz Seibert's reasoning in his question; Drew's own answer was that investors were understanding when Tactical closed in early 2023 after two long-time key employees retired.
correction.fix: Seibert argues that a liquid futures manager can return capital within 30 days, so a closure is a small event compared with illiquid strategies; Drew replies that Tactical closed in 2023 when two key employees retired, and that investors understood.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: they were a psychological support in addition to the person that found you
claims.claim: Commodities Corp recruited independent traders and gave each a staff contact who counselled and encouraged them through drawdowns, an institutional practice to keep skilled traders trading through losing periods.
claims.conditions: when a trader is in a drawdown

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: he always encouraged me to try to trade in a style more similar to his because he felt it was more profitable over the long run
claims.claim: Seykota believed technical discretionary pattern trading is more profitable over the long run than algorithmic systematic trading, although Drew never adopted it for his investors.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: small speculators are going to become irrelevant because the size that they trade is tiny compared to the size you might want to trade
claims.claim: A professional running funds cannot rely on small speculators as the source of profits because their size is too small for the capital deployed, so the large-capital edge has to come from commercial hedgers.
claims.testable: partly - COT groups can be tested

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: Now do I know that they actually did? No, I have no idea. But it's a it's a better basis for determining timing than just trying to guess that a trend is starting
claims.claim: Drew admits he never verified that hedgers actually shifted at the points his patterns flagged; the hedger-shift hypothesis was a better design basis for entry timing than guessing when a trend begins, so the edge was inferred rather than observed.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: just being able to never quit you know that's the thing you're you make a decision at the beginning I have faith in this method I'm not going to abandon the method
claims.claim: A volatile risk-premium strategy needs a decision at the outset to have faith in the method and never abandon it, because knocked-down-and-stand-up-again is how the hedger premium is earned and drawdowns of years are expected.
claims.conditions: long drawdowns without new equity highs

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: you always want to look back as far as you can if you're doing systematic trading
claims.claim: Systematic strategies should be tested on the longest possible history (Drew obtained 1970s Board of Trade charts and typed in the data by hand) to see markets and regimes such as 1970s potato trends.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: you want to have something in your portfolio that looks at what your portfolio is trying to achieve for you and make sure that you have some feedback on it
claims.claim: A portfolio should include a feedback mechanism that checks whether it still delivers its stated goal (such as smoother equity growth), not only a static basket of markets.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: it gives us an opportunity to also explain in more detail what it is that we do, how we trade, why the volatility exists, and that they need to be there for a period of time
claims.claim: A client base of private investors and family offices, rather than large institutions, lets the manager explain the volatility and the required holding period, reducing short-term redemptions.
claims.testable: partly - redemption data by investor type

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: then they have to dial their positions down and they have to respond to these investors and smooth the returns and v control stuff and avoid getting into a draw down otherwise they get fired
claims.claim: Large funds concentrated in interest-rate and equity markets (where it is risk-on/risk-off) are forced to dial positions down and control volatility to avoid drawdowns because investors will fire them, misaligning incentives and degrading the trend edge.
claims.conditions: when assets are very large and risk is concentrated in rates and equities

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: Some of these markets we can find in in China where they have markets that are very liquid, very large, markets that are difficult to access for say US persons and institutions
claims.claim: Chinese futures markets are very liquid, large and offer portfolio qualities (different contracts) not found on CME, but are difficult for US persons to reach; there are legitimate routes, making them a source of diversification.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: most most people most commodity traders stop trading because they blow up
claims.claim: Blowing up is the number one reason a long-lived commodity trading firm disappears, followed by ageing or death of the principals; Tactical closed instead because two key employees retired in 2023.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: your investors if you've selected them according to the criteria you've mentioned they will understand
claims.claim: Investors chosen for fit and informed about risks accept a closure or key-person event with understanding, while mismatched investors are likely to redeem at the low, so investor selection is itself risk management.
